doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

title: Wrong notes, Dizzy, Miles and responsive rhythm sections
summary: Any note can work if approached properly; Dizzy's intent versus Miles's, and adjusting to limited accompanists such as student groups.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Sure. I mean there are certain notes that sound better than others but to be honest any note can be played over any chord if it’s approached from the right note and leads to the right note.

So if you don’t, does it constitute — you know this term “wrong note” I know is debatable. But if you were teaching a lesson and someone’s playing a note that really doesn’t quite belong and they’re not either justifying it or setting it up. Would you say to that student, “that could be done better,” or something?

Oh of course, yes. And I would say it’s not a wrong note but it’s a wrong way to play that note over that chord. You know there’s a certain way to get to that note. If you’re going to just go for it and have it sound really wrong, which a lot of great players have done, you’ve got to have some way to skillfully tell everybody you meant to do that and it wasn’t a mistake. And you have to have the presence of mind, you have to be able to do that, and you have to be relaxed not to do that, and you have to be comfortable in your own skin enough. You know it’s like using the wrong word in a sentence. Some people might completely freeze up if they had the camera on them or in public speaking. You know, it’s the same type of thing. But if you know the word’s wrong and you kind of just correct yourself and move on it’s fine. Everyone understands what you were trying to say and it’s fine. Or to the extreme, look at someone like Norm Crosby. He knew exactly what he was talking about — I don’t know if you’re familiar with him, he’s a comedian. He was the king of the malapropisms. He would use the wrong word but you would still know what he was talking about. And it was funny because you knew it was the wrong word but you knew what he was talking about.

When I listen to some, any number of people, I think of Dizzy Gillespie sometimes. And sometimes he plays something and I go my God, I never would have thought of that. And it’s until you maybe listen to it again, it didn’t sound right.
Yeah. But what’s interesting with Dizzy, when you hear him play there is so much forethought in what he did. When he does those notes you can hear the intent. It’s not an

accident. And then there’s someone like Miles Davis, who in my mind I think he would intentionally play wrong notes to get his rhythm section to creatively find a way to make something happen. And that’s the thing. If you’re going to play those notes from out of the key or however you want to describe it, you need to have a sensitive rhythm section. If you have someone just banging out the chords — one-three-five-seven-nine — like this, and you play this stuff and they don’t follow you, it’s going to sound wrong, no matter how your intent is. So it’s got to be a give and take and that communication within the rhythm section too. The people that are accompanying you, if they don’t have the facility — like I’ve played with many groups — pick up groups — where you can just tell the piano player is not going to go there. No matter what you do. And sure you can do it, and you can feel good, okay this is my thing, I’m going to do my thing, but musically it doesn’t make sense. You know it’s like sitting in a room with three garbage men and trying to talk quantum physics. You know, you’re not going to have a good conversation. You may be a hundred percent right, but what’s it doing for the conversation? Nothing. So in those cases I just reel it back and I say okay well I’m just going to play more straight-ahead and enjoy being in that box tonight.
Um hum. And that is a challenge in itself.

Yeah. Yeah. And I learned a lot about doing that working with student groups. Because they don’t have a lot of facility. So you’ve got to be able to create interesting solos and something that feels different and fresh based upon very basic information that they’re supplying you as an accompaniment.
